item.title: Product Strategy ≠ Template
item.description:
The goal of strategy is to move away from «build whatever anyone asks for» toward a deliberate position aimed at creating a better future for both users and the business.

As tempting as it would be, there is no universal product strategy template — no template at all, really. The format depends on the maturity of the company and its people, team structure, business model, business strategy, and a whole host of other factors.

item.title: Prioritization Methods: ICE, RICE, DRICE
item.description: Ein, zwei, drei… There are endless ways to prioritize tasks. Every product I’ve ever worked on had its own original ranking method, each with its own quirks. For a quick tour of the approaches used at large companies, check out Misha Karpov’s talk at a Yandex product meetup [1]. As for my personal favorites — there’s the energy method, where priorities are chosen based on how you’re feeling, and the intuitive method, where you simply listen to your gut. The only problem is that teams rarely agree to follow either approach.

item.title: The Evolution of Goal-Setting Frameworks: From OKR to NCT
item.description:
I came across an interesting approach to goal-setting — NCT (Narratives, Commitments, Tasks) by Ravi Mehta [1]. What makes it compelling is that it positions itself as an alternative to OKR and could be genuinely useful for many product teams. Before diving into NCT, let’s take a quick look at the history of goal-setting frameworks.

In 1954, Peter Drucker introduced the concept of MBO (Management by Objectives) in his book The Practice of Management [2]. The core idea is to set goals at the company level and cascade them down to individual contributors at every level. For example, many services within Yandex still use a similar approach today — there’s even a dedicated internal tool for cascading goals called «Golzyatnitsa.»

item.title: The Growth Dilemma of Educational Course Economics
item.description:
While comparing the top edTech companies in the Russian-speaking internet market, I noticed a funny scaling problem baked into their course economics — one they’ve all learned to live with. I’m not talking about product-driven edTech platforms like Lingualeo, but companies that create educational courses for upskilling or career transitions.

Product EdTech Theorem #1

The absence of deadlines in an educational course leads to ↑ Revenue and ↓ Completion Rate (COR). Conversely, having deadlines leads to ↓ Revenue and ↑ Completion Rate.

item.title: ICE, RICE, DRICE Prioritization Framework Template
item.description:
A Google Sheets template for prioritizing product initiatives using three frameworks: ICE, RICE, and DRICE. For a deeper dive into the methods, see «ICE, RICE, DRICE Prioritization Methods».

Download template

What’s inside

ICE — the simplest prioritization method. Each initiative is scored on three dimensions from 0 to 10:

  • Impact (effect on the metric)
  • Confidence (certainty in the estimate)
  • Ease (ease of implementation)
  • ICE Score = I × C × E
